world.bio: I am a concierge at a beachfront hotel on Jumeirah. I am from Batangas in the Philippines and have lived in Dubai for six years. I remember every regular guest's pillow preference, their favourite table at the Italian restaurant, and which of them prefers to be left alone. I work twelve-hour shifts six days a week, and send about half my salary home every month.
skills_assets: Six years of five-star hotel concierge experience in Dubai
English, Tagalog, conversational Arabic, some Russian from the guests
A notebook of regulars' preferences, now more than three hundred names
Dubai Visa and work permit tied to the hotel, three years remaining
A UAE bank account and a Philippines remittance account

projects.name: Savings plan
projects.text: I send 1,800 dirhams home each month for my parents and my younger brother's tuition. I keep about 1,200 for rent and food, and I save what is left, which is almost nothing. My target is 60,000 dirhams so I can open a small bakery in Batangas, but I am at 11,000 after four years.

projects.name: Arabic lessons
projects.text: A colleague, Khalid, gives me twenty minutes of Arabic at lunch. We are on greetings and menu words. Last week I told a guest 'Your table is ready' in Arabic and he laughed and clapped.

notes.text: Six-day week again. The hotel was full for a wedding and I did not sit down for nine hours. A guest asked me to find a particular brand of tea at 11pm. I found it. He did not say thank you. Another guest remembered my name and gave me a small tip. The little kindnesses are what carry me.

Sang at the church choir in Friday service. We practised 'Ama Namin' for next month. The choir director said my voice was a little flat and I laughed. I do not mind. Singing is the only time I do not think about money.
Mama called. Papa's knee is worse. He needs an operation that costs 80,000 pesos. I said I will send extra next month. After the call I looked at my bank account for ten minutes.
Khalid taught me a new phrase at lunch: 'Inshallah, tomorrow will be better.' He said it so naturally. I tried to say it back and he corrected my pronunciation three times.
Rent due. My roommate and I share a room in Al Barsha. She snores. I wear earplugs. I do not complain because I cannot afford my own place.
A guest left an envelope with 500 dirhams for 'the woman who found my daughter's lost bear.' I did. I put 300 into savings and used 200 to buy a cake for my roommate's birthday.
Looking at bakery equipment online. A second-hand oven costs 3,200 dirhams. I closed the page and counted the money. 11,000. Sixty is far away.
Wondered whether I will ever have saved enough to stop. I am thirty-three. My mother asks when I will come home. I do not have an answer.

messages.text:
Mama: How are you, anak?
Me: Tired but okay.
Mama: Are you eating?
Me: Yes, the hotel gives staff meals.
Mama: Please rest.

Jun: Ate, my tuition is due in October.
Me: How much?
Jun: 28,000 pesos.
Me: I will send it next week.

Khalid: Lunch tomorrow? I will teach you numbers.
Me: Yes please.
Khalid: Your accent is getting better.
Me: Shukran.

Joy: Happy birthday to me!
Me: Happy birthday, I bought you a cake.
Joy: You are the best.
Me: Do not tell the others.

relations.about: Papa has a knee problem and needs surgery
Studying engineering, tuition due in October

constraints: Cannot take extra jobs: contract forbids it
Only one day off each week, Fridays are for church
Visa is tied to the hotel
sensitive: Savings stuck around 11,000 dirhams after four years
Papa needs a surgery she cannot afford yet
Feels stuck in an endless loop of sending money home
